title: In Defense of Memory: Why Remembering Is a Social Justice Issue
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Prompted by a question about how memory became demonised in education, Hughes traces the genealogy of anti-memorisation sentiment and then argues it has an equity cost. She identifies four sources: centuries of recitation that made memory symbolically synonymous with obedience, Rousseau's romantic opposition of natural discovery to artificial imposition, mid-century psychology's framing of recall as surface performance beneath 'real' thinking, and the critique of the canon that made memorisation look like cultural exclusion. Her repeated move is to separate the object from its historical use: it was the use of memory for indoctrination that was the problem, not memory itself. She then brings cognitive science to bear - Willingham's memory as the residue of thought, prior knowledge predicting comprehension, expertise as organised retrievable knowledge, and the failure of domain-general critical thinking to transfer. The equity turn is the Matthew Effect: inquiry and project-based approaches without systematic knowledge-building advantage pupils who already have vocabulary and background knowledge, so explicit teaching for memory is what levels the field. GCSE English is her worked example, where interpretive power depends on what can be retrieved under exam conditions, and she ends by pressing the 2025 Curriculum and Assessment Review to reject the knowledge-versus-skills dichotomy.
points: The historical argument is the piece's distinctive contribution: memory was discredited by association with recitation, obedience and canon enforcement, none of which are intrinsic to remembering.

Hughes's rebuttal of the 'why remember when you can look it up' position is that comprehension requires internalised knowledge, recognition is not recall, and external tools amplify cognition without replacing it.
The Matthew Effect framing inverts the usual politics: knowledge-light pedagogy is presented as the regressive option, because it silently rewards the pupils who arrived already equipped.
GCSE English is used as the concrete case - quotations, structures, genre conventions and contextual knowledge must be retrievable or critical analysis collapses under exam conditions.

She notes that marginalised communities have themselves used memory - oral histories, songs, speeches - as a tool of survival and resistance, and that Freire criticised uncritical memorisation without rejecting memory.
quotes: In UK education, memorisation has often been treated with suspicion. Phrases like “Don’t memorise, understand” or curriculum reforms favouring abstract skills over knowledge have framed memory as outdated, oppressive and at times irrelevant.

For centuries, schooling in Europe emphasised recitation and memorisation of religious texts, laws and classical works. By the 19th century, this model was increasingly seen as authoritarian, stifling creativity and designed to produce compliant citizens and workers. So memory became symbolically linked to submission, even though memorisation and submission are not inherently connected.

While these concerns stem from a genuine desire to promote equity and empower learners, research demonstrates that memory is not the enemy of understanding, creativity, or social justice—it is foundational to them. Neglecting memory inadvertently advantages students who already possess background knowledge and cultural capital.
This is a false opposition. In reality, you cannot think critically about what you do not remember and skills are executed through stored knowledge. But slogans are easier than nuance.

Willingham (2009) notes that memory is the ‘residue of thought,’ meaning we remember what we think about. He emphasises that thinking hard about something is crucial for learning it, as memory isn't a storage tank but an outcome of mental processing, not passive reception. Students cannot analyse texts, solve problems, or reason critically without retrieving stored facts, concepts and schemas.

Success depends on what they can retrieve from memory: quotations/references, narrative structures, genre conventions, contextual knowledge, and vocabulary. Without this, critical analysis may collapse.

A curriculum that assumes discovery without structured knowledge-building risks perpetuating inequality. In contrast, one that values retrieval, cumulative knowledge, and shared cultural literacy, while remaining pluralistic and critically aware, promotes cognitive justice.
